abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic framework for visual perception that fundamentally reinterprets object detection and image segmentation as probabilistic inference problems within a unified entropy minimization paradigm. Unlike conventional deep learning approaches that rely on empirical risk minimization, our theoretical analysis establishes that visual recognition emerges naturally from minimizing the conditional entropy between visual features and semantic labels across multiple scales. We prove that the proposed framework provides strict bounds on recognition accuracy that are independent of network architecture, offering a new theoretical lens for understanding deep learning for vision. The framework introduces the concept of perceptual redundancy reduction, where visual tracking and motion analysis are reformulated as iterative entropy reduction processes operating on spatio-temporal feature manifolds. By deriving closed-form solutions for the optimal feature representations under this paradigm, we demonstrate that traditional convolutional operations can be replaced with theoretically optimal linear transforms that maximize mutual information between input pixels and high-level semantic concepts. Experimental validation on standard benchmarks for scene understanding demonstrates that models derived from this paradigm achieve state-of-the-art performance while providing theoretical guarantees on generalization bounds. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation that bridges computer vision with statistical learning theory, offering profound implications for future research in visual intelligence.

We present a rigorous theoretical analysis of the optimization dynamics in deep neural networks for image understanding tasks, establishing novel convergence guarantees that significantly improve upon existing bounds. Our analysis reveals that the empirical observation of benign overfitting in modern vision architectures can be theoretically explained through the lens of implicit regularization, where gradient descent on exponential loss families induces a data-dependent bias toward low-complexity solutions. We derive refined PAC-Bayes bounds for visual recognition that account for the hierarchical feature composition inherent in convolutional architectures, demonstrating that the commonly used spectral norm regularization is insufficient for controlling generalization error in deep networks. By introducing a novel measure of visual complexity based on the covering number of the data manifold, we establish tighter risk bounds for object detection and semantic segmentation that depend on the intrinsic dimensionality of image distributions rather than raw pixel dimensions. Our theoretical framework provides specific conditions under which scene understanding models achieve optimal sample complexity, offering actionable guidelines for architecture design. Experimental results on standard benchmarks confirm that networks designed according to our theoretical principles achieve measurable improvements in both in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness, validating the practical significance of our theoretical contributions to the field of computer vision.

We introduce a groundbreaking multi-modal neural architecture that fundamentally transforms the paradigm for 3D reconstruction and scene understanding by jointly processing visual, depth, and semantic cues through a unified transformer-based framework. The proposed system, termed VisionTransformer3D (VT3D), abandons the traditional pipeline of sequential feature extraction followed by post-processing, instead employing a hierarchical attention mechanism that enables direct reasoning about object detection, spatial relationships, and geometric structure within a single end-to-end trainable architecture. Our system design addresses the long-standing challenge of coupling 3D reconstruction with semantic understanding by introducing cross-modal attention blocks that dynamically weight contributions from different sensor modalities based on their reliability in specific scene contexts. The architecture incorporates novel positional encoding schemes that respect the Euclidean geometry of 3D space while maintaining computational efficiency for high-resolution scene representations. For visual tracking and motion analysis, we propose a temporal attention module that maintains object identities across video frames without explicit re-identification modules. Extensive evaluation on challenging datasets for autonomous navigation and augmented reality demonstrates that VT3D achieves unprecedented accuracy in dense 3D scene reconstruction while simultaneously providing rich semantic annotations. This work establishes a new paradigm for integrated visual perception systems that unifies previously separate computer vision tasks.

This paper presents a highly efficient and accurate system for real-time object detection and instance segmentation that achieves significant improvements in speed-accuracy trade-offs through innovative architectural modifications and training strategies. Our proposed framework, called LightSegNet, addresses the computational bottlenecks in modern visual recognition systems by introducing a novel feature fusion module that combines high-level semantic information with low-level spatial details through learnable cross-scale connections, eliminating the need for costly feature pyramids. The system design incorporates a new anchor-free detection head that reduces the memory footprint by 60% compared to anchor-based alternatives while maintaining competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks. For video analysis tasks including action recognition and visual tracking, we develop a temporal difference attention mechanism that captures motion patterns with minimal computational overhead, achieving a threefold improvement in inference speed for video understanding pipelines. Our training methodology combines knowledge distillation from large-scale pretrained models with a novel data augmentation strategy specifically designed for image segmentation that preserves boundary information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LightSegNet achieves 42.3 FPS on embedded hardware for object detection and instance segmentation at 768×768 resolution, with accuracy improvements of 2.1% mAP over previous state-of-the-art real-time methods. This work provides a practical solution for deploying sophisticated visual perception capabilities on resource-constrained platforms.
